newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: REPO AUCTION START LOW KEY BUT BANKS APPROVE.
newsitem.headline: REPO AUCTION START LOW KEY BUT BANKS APPROVE.

text.p: Lithuanian banks on Thursday said they welcomed the start of repo auctions by the Bank of Lithuania although the first auction was under-subscribed.
The central bank on Wednesday launched its first repurchase auction, buying back 300,000 litas of government T-bills with a seven percent annual interest rate with a term of seven days.
The auction was the first step in the bank's policy of more active management of money markets and, eventually, the litas.

The director of market operations at the Bank of Lithuania, Arvydas Kregzhde, told Reuters the first repo auction should be considered as a move to master the technique rather than putting the bank's monetary policy into operation.
He said only one bank participated in the first auction.
"We think that in the future other commercial banks will use this financial instrument with more confidence to administrate their liquidity," Kregzhde added.
Commercial bankers mostly agreed the repo auction was a good idea although one said its technicalities needed to be changed.

"We did not take part in the auction but intend to use this financial instrument in the future. It will allow us better to administer assets and liquidity," the head of Hermis Bank's treasury department, Vytautas Palijanskas, told Reuters.
Litimpeks Bank also had little doubt about the necessity of repo auctions at this stage of the banking sector's development.

"If trust between the banks, damaged by the 1995 banking crisis, can be restored and the interbank loan market function normally, the need for repo auctions would be less," said Raimonda Kezhiene, the head of Litimpeks Bank's treasury.
"I welcome this auction as a new product of the Bank of Lithuania," the head of the treasury department of Vilnaius Bank, Romualdas Chesnavichius, said.
"But it is not efficient enough as the repurchase term is very short and the payment has to be made next day," he added.
"At the moment, the demand for T-bills is very high on the market and banks prefer to sell them on the secondary market rather than take part in the auction," he said.
